2.why: A, B and D are three parallel era-facts; C is the only option that generalizes across them into a trend, and it is the only one carrying the terminal datum (1888 roll film).

3.why: A, B, C are isolated notes; D is the only option with a cause-and-effect chain that subsumes them (depletion + pests -> rotation).

4.why: B supplies pitch, A supplies travel distance, and D is the only option that fuses the two into one mechanism; C is setup periphery.

5.why: Only option holding two measures in tension (self-rated alertness vs objective reaction time); A is half of it, C and D are periphery.

6.why: A and D are the two experiments' results and B is the only option that states what they jointly establish ('taken together ... confirmed').

7.why: C is method, D is caveats, A is an extension; B is the only option stating the headline datum and naming its magnitude, the summative shape this batch uses for keys.

8.why: C fuses D's sampling with B's bacteria into the finding, but A is an equally well-made purpose-statement and only the withheld stem could separate them.

9.why: A and B are the two single figures and C is the only option that sets them side by side in one sentence; D generalizes without using either number.

10.why: C is the bare central finding and B is finding+sample-limitation; I bet against the limitation family, but C does not integrate anything, so this is the rule's weakest application.

11.why: A contradicts, B and C are single details; D is the only option aggregating the studies into a consistent result.

12.why: B carries the numeric outcome and the duration where D is the same claim stripped of data, but B's trailing 'the outcome researchers measured' reads like author padding, so I am not sure which of B/D is the key.

13.why: C is a deliberately over-drawn generalization from the single exception, which suggests a generalization stem whose correctly hedged counterpart is A - but D's mechanism synthesis is the shape I called the key elsewhere, so the two rules disagree here.

14.why: A, C, D are single figures from separate sources; B is the only option converging three independent methods on one value.

15.why: D is one study, A adds an unrelated outcome, B states consistency only; C is the sole cause-to-consequence chain (hippocampus + BDNF -> memory scores).

18.why: C and D are two co-equal limitations, so a limitation stem would be ambiguous; by determinacy the key should be the finding, A - but that is an inference about the author, not about the values.

20.why: A folds B's twelve vents and C's food-web role into one hedged generalization with the exception handled by D - but C is the mechanism option, which is the key shape I chose in the parallel item 13's sibling reading.

21.why: D is C's over-drawn twin, which usually marks C's content as the key's, yet A is a well-made causation caution that would be the key under an entirely different stem; coin-flip between A and C.

22.why: A is the only explicit causal explanation (ash weathers -> minerals -> fertility), but C is the option that actually combines both notes (minerals and Java), so integration and causality point different ways.

23.why: A, B, C are single measurements or method; D is the only option that compares the two periods and quantifies the acceleration.

24.why: A, C, D each pair two of the effects; B is the umbrella option naming the common cause and all three effects at once.
